     7	LaTeX source (for example `P:clock-copy-obstruction`). The ledger was written

    11	`L:spatial-fourier-bound` (lines 101-164, display `E:spatial-fourier-bound`),

     3	## The paper's argument and where Lean enters
     4	
     5	The paper bounds and identifies the growth of `log E[u(t,x)²]` for the
     6	Stratonovich hyperbolic Anderson model. The argument has three layers.
     7	
     8	1. **Stochastic and analytic layer.** The chaos expansion, the two-chain
     9	   pairing integrals, Wick pairings (beyond finite families of Gaussian
    10	   values), Gaussian integration (beyond finitely many standard Gaussians),
    11	   imported bounds,
    12	   Laplace transforms and the variational asymptotics. **Not in Lean**,
    13	   except a few slices: the Laplace transforms of the wave kernel and of
    14	   the two-time kernel and the subordination formula (`ClockCopy` and its
    15	   foundation modules), the Gaussian transform of the spectral measure
    16	   (`MaskedSpectralGrowth`), the uniform scalar frequency row
    17	   (`FrequencyRow`), the temporal completion `H_a` (`TimeCompletion`), the
    18	   auxiliary mask norm (`MaskedAuxiliaryNorm`), the Gaussian heat envelope
    19	   of the covariance (`VariationalMean`), a finite Hilbert-valued Bessel
    20	   inequality (`PhaseBessel`), the wave Green measures `G_s` for
    21	   `d = 1, 2, 3` (`WaveGreen`), the spectral identity and positive
    22	   definiteness of `Gamma = delta_0(dx_1) dx_2` (`QuotientObstruction`), a
    23	   finite Gaussian comparison under the positive semidefinite order
    24	   (`GaussianComparison`), the two wave variance directions in spectral
    25	   form (`WaveTwoVariances`), the variational floor and the Rayleigh-form
    26	   rate (`VariationalFloor`, `VariationalRate`), the deterministic Fourier
    27	   bound `L:spatial-fourier-bound` for the smooth spatial ratio and the
    28	   static controls
    29	   (`SpatialFourierBound`, `SpatialSmoothRatio`, `SpatialStaticControls`,
    30	   `SpatialOccupationCompleted`), series types and the continuity of the
    31	   growth types in the temporal exponent (`SeriesType`, `TypeContinuity`),
    32	   the white-noise bound formulas and clock transforms
    33	   (`WhiteRelativeWidth`, `WhiteClockLaplace`), the coefficient bound of
    34	   the interval inventory product (`InventoryProduct`), an abstract `L^2`
    35	   limit of a regularized series under a uniform scaled moment bound
    36	   (`UniformSeriesTail`), the density of test functions in the
    37	   weak-gradient `H^1` (`H1Density`), the physical four-linear extension
    38	   and the spatial energy (`SpatialFourLinear`), the full physical
    39	   occupation class (`OccupationPhysicalClass`; both completed in
    40	   `SpatialOccupationL7Completed`), the scalar and Hilbert-space steps
    41	   of the static interaction and interval coefficient bounds
    42	   (`IntervalScalar`, `IntervalScalarCompleted`), the spectral-mass
    43	   identity `R_Gamma(1) = R_alpha` (`SpectralMassIdentity`), Gaussian
    44	   smoothing as a Fourier multiplier (`DampedMultiplier`), the positivity of
    45	   the space-time occupation form, the deterministic occupation ceiling and
    46	   the spatial bracket (`SpaceTimePositivity`, `OccupationCeilingFinite`,
    47	   `SpatialBracket`, completed in `L8Completed`), the masked rates
    48	   (`RemoveMask`), the finite Wick formula and the terminal-chain Wick
    49	   formula with the chain measures given by their masses (`FiniteWick`,
    50	   `TerminalWick`), an abstract compact Young baseline (`SymplecticFree`)
    51	   and the Cauchy steps of the static phase orders (`StaticPhaseCauchy`),
    52	   the Fourier transforms of the wave Green measures in `d = 1, 2, 3` and
    53	   Archimedes' law for the sphere measure (`WaveGreenFourier`), the low-alpha
    54	   convolution bound and the static contraction bounds
    55	   (`LowAlphaConvolution`, `PhaseContractions`, completed in `L9Completed`),
    56	   the exact occupation constant and ceiling (`RawOccupationEnergy`,
    57	   `OccupationCeilingExact`), the normalized Hermite polynomials and the
    58	   finite Gaussian Fock layer with values in a Hilbert factor
    59	   (`GaussianHermite`, `HermiteFock`) and their consumers `L:fock-form`,
    60	   `L:interval-contractions` and `E:occupied-multiplication` (`FockForm`),
    61	   and the scalar and numerical-range steps of the complex phase bounds
    62	   (`ComplexPhaseScalar`).
    63	2. **Reductions to explicit inequalities.** At many points the analytic
    64	   argument reduces to a finite statement: an exponent range, an exact
    65	   rational or square-root inequality, a polynomial that must stay positive
    66	   on a region, a determinant or matrix inverse, a count of coefficients in
    67	   a finite word, or an integral comparison once integrability is known.
    68	   **These are what Lean checks.**
    69	3. **Assembly** of the main theorems from the layers above. **Not in Lean.**
    70	
    71	So each module checks one reduction in layer 2. Its hypotheses state the
    72	facts that layer 1 supplies (for example positivity of a parameter,
    73	integrability of a function, or an inequality proved analytically in the
    74	paper). Its conclusion is the fact that the paper then uses.

   128	## Reading a statement
   129	
   130	For each declaration, check three things against the paper:
   131	
   132	1. the hypotheses match what the paper has available at that point;
   133	2. the conclusion is what the paper uses next;
   134	3. parameter ranges, strict versus non-strict inequalities and quantifier
   135	   order agree.
   136	
   137	The [statement ledger](docs/statement-ledger.md) records this for every row.
   138	`Audit/<module>/` prints the full elaborated types, so the statements can be
   139	read without opening an editor.

   142

   146	and will be added here when that library is released.

     3	  210| We study the hyperbolic Anderson model
     4	  211| \cite{chen:author2026:time-dependency}*{(1.1)}
     5	  212| \begin{equation}\label{E:HAM}
     6	  213|   \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2}(t,x)=\Delta u(t,x)+\W(t,x)u(t,x),
     7	  214|   \qquad u(0,x)=1,\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(0,x)=0,
     8	  215| \end{equation}
     9	  216| for $(t,x) \in \R_+\times\R^d$, $d \in \{1,2,3\}$, interpreted in the
    10	  217| Stratonovich sense (limit of classical wave equations driven by smoothed noises
    11	  218| $\W_{\epsilon,\delta}$). The noise is centered Gaussian with
    12	  219| \begin{equation}\label{E:cov}
    13	  220|   \operatorname{Cov}\big(\W(s,x),\W(t,y)\big)=|s-t|^{-\alpha_0}\gamma(x-y),
    14	  221|   \qquad 0<\alpha_0<1,
    15	  222| \end{equation}
    16	  223| where $\gamma \ge 0$ is nonnegative definite with spectral measure $\mu$.
    17	  224| 
    18	  225| \begin{hypothesis}[Homogeneous covariance]\label{H:homog}
    19	  226|   Let $d \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $0 < \alpha_0 < 1$. The spatial covariance is a
    20	  227|   nonnegative, even, positive-definite tempered Radon measure $\Gamma$ on
    21	  228|   $\R^d$, with positive even tempered Radon spectral measure $\mu$ in the
    22	  229|   convention
    23	  230|   \[
    24	  231|     \Gamma=\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}\mu(\ud\xi)
    25	  232|     \quad\text{in the sense of tempered distributions}.
    26	  233|   \]
    27	  234|   The symbol $\gamma$ in~\eqref{E:cov} denotes this covariance as a function
    28	  235|   when one exists, and as a distribution otherwise. For every Borel set $A$ and
    29	  236|   $c > 0$, $\Gamma(cA) = c^{d-\alpha}\Gamma(A)$, and
    30	  237|   \begin{equation}\label{E:threshold}
    31	  238|     \alpha_0+\alpha<2,
    32	  239|   \end{equation}
    33	  240|   with $0 < \alpha < d$, or $\alpha = d = 1$. In particular, the last case
    34	  241|   includes spatial white noise $\Gamma = \delta_0$.
    35	  242| \end{hypothesis}
    36	  243| 
    37	  244| \paragraph{Zero covariance.}

    68	  803| \begin{lemma}[Homogeneous damped norms and temporal tails]
    69	  804|   \label{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}
    70	  805|   Under Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, the integrals
    71	  806|   in~\eqref{E:damped-norm-definitions} are finite for every $\theta > 0$, with
    72	  807|   $N_2(\theta)^2 \ge 0$, and
    73	  808|   \[
    74	  809|     N_0(\theta)=\theta^{-2},\qquad
    75	  810|     N_1(\theta)=\theta^{\alpha+\alpha_0-2}N_1(1),\qquad
    76	  811|     N_2(\theta)^2=\theta^{-\beta}N_2(1)^2,
    77	  812|     \quad\beta=4-\alpha-\alpha_0.
    78	  813|   \]
    79	  814|   Let
    80	  815|   \[
    81	  816|     K_M(r)=\frac1{\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(\alpha_0)}
    82	  817|     \int_M^\infty e^{-\lambda|r|}\lambda^{\alpha_0-1}\ud\lambda.
    83	  818|   \]
    84	  819|   Denote by $N_1^{(M)}(1)$ the first norm with $\lambda > M$, and by
    85	  820|   $N_2^{(M)}(1)$ the second norm with $K_M(s-t)$ in place of
    86	  821|   $|s-t|^{-\alpha_0}$. Then
    87	  822|   \begin{equation}\label{E:damped-tail-norms}
    88	  823|     N_1^{(M)}(1)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
    89	  824|     N_2^{(M)}(1)\longrightarrow0\quad(M\to\infty).
    90	  825|   \end{equation}

    92	  827|   $S\subset S'\subset(0,\infty)$ be measurable. Define $N_{1,m,S}(\theta)$
    93	  828|   by replacing $\mu$ with $m\mu$ and restricting the $\lambda$ integral in

    95	  830|   and the temporal kernel in $N_2^2$ with
    96	  831|   \[
    97	  832|     K_S(r)=\frac1{\Gamma_{\mathrm{E}}(\alpha_0)}
    98	  833|     \int_S e^{-\lambda|r|}\lambda^{\alpha_0-1}\ud\lambda.

   695	  350| \subsection{The kernel row and full occupation energy}
   696	  351| 
   697	  352| Define, for $u \ne 0$,
   698	  353| \begin{equation}\label{E:occupation-damped-kernel}
   699	  354|   K_\star(u)=\frac1{\Gamma_E(a)}
   700	  355|   \int_0^\infty
   701	  356|   e^{-(\lambda+\lambda^2/(2D))|u|}
   702	  357|   \lambda^{a-1}\ud\lambda,
   703	  358| \end{equation}
   704	  359| and set $K_\star(0) = 0$ for time integration.
   705	  360| 
   706	  361| \begin{lemma}[Exact row maximum]\label{L:occupation-kernel-row}
   707	  362|   The kernel is even, positive off zero, locally integrable, decreasing on
   708	  363|   $(0,\infty)$, and $K_\star(u) \le |u|^{-a}$ off zero. Its exact row maximum on
   709	  364|   $[0,1]$ is
   710	  365|   \begin{equation}\label{E:occupation-kernel-row}
   711	  366|     \max_{s\in[0,1]}\int_0^1K_\star(s-t)\ud t
   712	  367|     =R_\star:=2\int_0^{1/2}K_\star(u)\ud u\in(0,\infty).
   713	  368|   \end{equation}
   714	  369| \end{lemma}
   715	  370| 
   716	  371| \begin{proof}
   717	  372|   Dropping the positive quadratic damping bounds the mixture by the Gamma
   718	  373|   integral $|u|^{-a}$. Positivity and monotonicity follow directly from the
   719	  374|   integrand, and $a < 1$ gives local integrability. Put $\Phi(t) =
   720	  375|   \int_0^tK_\star(u)\ud u$. It is concave because its integrand is decreasing on
   721	  376|   positive arguments. The row is $\Phi(s)+\Phi(1-s) \le 2\Phi(1/2)$, with
   722	  377|   equality at $s = 1/2$. The diagonal value changes no time integral. This
   723	  378|   proves Lemma~\ref{L:occupation-kernel-row}.

   188	\begin{proposition}[Completion on the same noise]\label{P:masked-noise-completion}
   189	  The space $\mathcal{D}$ belongs to the original test-noise completion and
   190	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-actual-noise-norm}
   191	    \E W(F)^2 = (2\pi)^d\int
   192	    \|\widehat{F}(\xi)\|_{H_a^{\mathbb{C}}}^2\mu(\ud\xi).
   193	  \end{equation}
   194	  Define the auxiliary seminorm
   195	  \[
   196	    N_R(F)^2 = (2\pi)^d\int
   197	    \|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_{H_a^{\mathbb{C}}}^2\nu_R(\ud\eta).
   198	  \]
   199	  Then $F \mapsto W(\zeta_RF)$ extends as a contraction from the null-quotient
   200	  completion for $N_R$ into the original $L^2(\Omega)$. The extension is
   201	  centered and jointly Gaussian. For finitely many real $F_1,\ldots,F_m \in
   202	  \mathcal{D}$, their masked covariance matrix is bounded in positive
   203	  semidefinite order by the matrix of auxiliary inner products. This gives
   204	  covariance comparison for every finite linear Gaussian image and every convex
   205	  norm power $p \ge 1$.
   206	\end{proposition}
   207	
   208	\begin{proof}
   209	  For real spatial Schwartz $f,g$, put $h(z) = \int f(y+z)g(y)\ud y$. Fourier
   210	  inversion and Parseval give
   211	  \[
   212	    h(z) = \int e^{i\xi\cdot z}\widehat{f}(\xi)
   213	    \overline{\widehat{g}(\xi)}\ud\xi.
   214	  \]
   215	  Therefore,
   216	  \[
   217	    \int e^{i\xi\cdot z}h(z)\ud z
   218	    = (2\pi)^d\widehat{f}(-\xi)\overline{\widehat{g}(-\xi)}.
   219	  \]
   220	  Apply~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to the single test $h$ and reflect
   221	  $\xi$ using evenness of $\mu$. The spatial covariance is thus
   222	  $(2\pi)^d\int\widehat{f}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{g}(\xi)}\mu(\ud\xi)$. Summing
   223	  over the finitely many temporal factors gives
   224	  \eqref{E:masked-actual-noise-norm}. Schwartz decay, temperedness and temporal
   225	  integrability justify these pairings. If $W$ is initially given only on
   226	  compact spatial tests, smooth expanding cutoffs converge in the Schwartz
   227	  topology. The spectral form is continuous in that topology, admitting
   228	  $\mathcal{D}$ in the same completion.
   229	
   230	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}, applied with $H =
   231	  H_a^{\mathbb{C}}$, gives $\E W(\zeta_RF)^2 \le N_R(F)^2$. It annihilates
   232	  auxiliary-null tests. An auxiliary Cauchy sequence thus gives a Cauchy
   233	  sequence of noise evaluations in $L^2(\Omega)$, proving the contraction
   234	  extension and its uniqueness. Every finite linear combination of the limits is
   235	  an $L^2$ limit of centered Gaussian variables. Their variances converge, so
   236	  their characteristic functions prove that the limits remain jointly centered
   237	  Gaussian.
   238	
   239	  For the finite family let $A$ be the covariance matrix and $B$ the auxiliary
   240	  Gram matrix. Applying the norm inequality to $\sum_i b_iF_i$ gives
   241	  $b^{\mathsf{T}}Ab \le b^{\mathsf{T}}Bb$ for every real vector $b$.
   242	  Diagonalizing $B-A$ constructs a centered Gaussian vector $Z$ of that
   243	  covariance, independent of the evaluation vector $X$, on a product space. Then
   244	  $X+Z$ has covariance $B$. Conditional Jensen gives $\E\|X\|^p \le \E\|X+Z\|^p$
   245	  for every norm and $p \ge 1$. Finite Gaussian moments ensure finiteness of
   246	  both sides. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:masked-noise-completion}.
   247	\end{proof}

    23	\begin{lemma}[Gaussian envelope for the original covariance]
    24	  \label{L:variational-heat-envelope}
    25	  For the normalized heat kernel $p_\epsilon(x) =
    26	  (2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/(2\epsilon)}$,
    27	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-heat-envelope}
    28	    (\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(x)
    29	    =\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2/2}\mu(\ud\xi),
    30	    \qquad
    31	    0\le(\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(x)
    32	    \le(\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(0)<\infty.
    33	  \end{equation}
    34	  The value at zero is strictly positive.
    35	\end{lemma}
    36	
    37	\begin{proof}
    38	  A positive tempered Radon measure has polynomial ball growth. Indeed, evaluate
    39	  its tempered bound on a nonnegative smooth cutoff equal to one on $B_1$,
    40	  dilated by $R \ge 1$. Its finitely many Schwartz seminorms are bounded by
    41	  $CR^N$, so positivity gives a ball-mass bound $CR^N$. Summing dyadic annuli
    42	  shows that $(1+|x|)^{-L}$ is integrable for $L > N$. Apply this separately to
    43	  $\Gamma$ and $\mu$. Gaussian weights are therefore integrable against both
    44	  measures. The classical convolution on the left is finite and smooth locally
    45	  in $x$: on compact $x$ sets its translated Gaussian derivatives are bounded by
    46	  any fixed sufficiently fast polynomial weight in the integration variable.
    47	
    48	  Pair the convolution with a Schwartz test $\varphi$. Absolute Fubini is
    49	  justified by these weights. The resulting pairing is that of $\Gamma$ with
    50	  $p_\epsilon*\varphi$. Applying the spectral convention in
    51	  Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} and the identity $\int p_\epsilon(y)e^{-i\xi\cdot
    52	  y}\ud y = e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2/2}$ gives exactly the right side
    53	  of~\eqref{E:variational-heat-envelope} as a distribution. The heat kernel is
    54	  even, so either Fourier sign gives that same Gaussian multiplier. Its spectral
    55	  integral is absolutely finite and continuous in $x$ by dominated convergence.
    56	  Thus, equality of the two continuous distributions gives equality at every
    57	  $x$, without an extra normalization factor. The physical convolution is
    58	  nonnegative. Evenness of $\mu$ makes the spectral integral real, and its
    59	  absolute value is bounded by its total Gaussian mass, the value at zero.
    60	  Finally, $\Gamma \ne 0$ and $p_\epsilon > 0$ give strict positivity there.
    61	  This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-heat-envelope}.
    62	\end{proof}

    64	\begin{lemma}[Global regularity of the original mean]
    65	  \label{L:variational-global-mean}
    66	  Every mixed time and space derivative of $h_s$ is globally bounded in space,
    67	  uniformly on compact time intervals. In particular, for $I = [0,1]$ there are
    68	  finite constants $M,C_\Psi$ such that
    69	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-global-mean}

    71	    \|h_s-h_t\|_\infty\le C_\Psi|s-t|,
    72	    \qquad s,t\in I.
    73	  \end{equation}
    74	\end{lemma}

    76	\begin{proof}

    80	  C_Dp_\epsilon(x)$ for all $t,x$. Here the heat kernel has a positive minimum

    82	  $\Gamma*|D\Psi(t,\cdot)|$ uniformly in $t,x$. Ordinary local differentiation
    83	  against the Radon measure gives the corresponding derivatives of the
    84	  convolution. After the change $r = s-t$,

    86	    h_s(x)=\int_\R |r|^{-a}

    88	  \]

    91	  1$. Every derivative thus falls on the smooth test and passes through the
    92	  integral by dominated convergence, with the claimed global spatial bounds.
    93	  Nonnegativity follows from positive kernels. The bounded time derivative
    94	  proves the Lipschitz estimate. No directional decay of the mean has been
    95	  inferred. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-global-mean}.
    96	\end{proof}
    97	
    98	\begin{proposition}[The unmasked Rayleigh rate]
    99	  \label{P:variational-unmasked-rate}
   100	  On complex $L^2(\R^d)$, the operator $H_s = -\Delta-h_s$ is self-adjoint on
   101	  $H^2$, with form domain $H^1$ and form $q_s(f) = \|\nabla f\|_2^2-\int
   102	  h_s|f|^2$. Its spectral bottom $E_s$ is uniformly negative on $I$. The
   103	  positive rate $\lambda_{\Psi,s} = \sqrt{-E_s}$ satisfies
   104	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-real-rayleigh}
   105	    \lambda_{\Psi,s}^2
   106	    =\sup_{\substack{f\in H^1(\R^d;\R)\\\|f\|_2=1}}
   107	    \left(\int h_sf^2-\|\nabla f\|_2^2\right).
   108	  \end{equation}
   109	  It is Lipschitz on $I$, and $I_\Psi: = \int_0^1\lambda_{\Psi,s}\ud s$ is
   110	  positive and finite. No eigenstate at the unmasked bottom is asserted.
   111	\end{proposition}
   112	
   113	\begin{proof}
   114	  The Fourier Laplacian $A = -\Delta$ is self-adjoint on $H^2$, being
   115	  multiplication by $|\xi|^2$ with its maximal domain. Multiplication $B_s =
   116	  -h_s$ is bounded self-adjoint with norm at most $M$. Thus, $H_s = A+B_s$ is
   117	  densely defined, symmetric and closed on $H^2$; the two graph norms are
   118	  equivalent under a bounded perturbation. For real $b > M$,
   119	  \[
   120	    H_s-ib=(I+B_s(A-ib)^{-1})(A-ib).
   121	  \]
   122	  The first factor has a Neumann inverse because $\|B_s(A-ib)^{-1}\| \le M/b <
   123	  1$, and the same holds with $+ib$. To check self-adjointness directly, for $u
   124	  \in D(H_s^*)$ solve $(H_s-ib)v = (H_s^*-ib)u$ with $v \in D(H_s)$. Then $u-v
   125	  \in \ker(H_s^*-ib) = \operatorname{Ran}(H_s+ib)^\perp = \{0\}$. Hence,
   126	  $D(H_s^*) = D(H_s)$.
   127	
   128	  Set $c_{\mathrm{shift}} = 1+M$ and $J_s = H_s+c_{\mathrm{shift}} \ge 1$.
   129	  Integration by parts on $H^2$ gives
   130	  \[
   131	    \|J_s^{1/2}f\|_2^2=q_s(f)+c_{\mathrm{shift}}\|f\|_2^2,\qquad
   132	    \|f\|_{H^1}^2\le\|J_s^{1/2}f\|_2^2
   133	    \le c_{\mathrm{shift}}\|f\|_{H^1}^2.
   134	  \]
   135	  Spectral cutoffs $1_{[1,n]}(J_s)$ show that $H^2 = D(J_s)$ is a core for the
   136	  half-power norm; Fourier cutoffs give its density in $H^1$. Completion in the
   137	  equivalent norms identifies $D(J_s^{1/2})$ and $H^1$ as $L^2$ subspaces, since
   138	  both norms dominate $L^2$. This proves the stated form domain.
   139	
   140	  The spectral lower bound gives one direction of the Rayleigh identity. For the
   141	  reverse, nonzero spectral projections in $[E_s,E_s+\epsilon]$ give unit $H^2$
   142	  vectors with Rayleigh values at most $E_s+\epsilon$. The bottom is finite
   143	  because the operator is bounded below and has finite Rayleigh tests. Let
   144	  $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Real tests give the same infimum: $q_s(u+iv) =
   145	  q_s(u)+q_s(v)$, so the quotient is the norm-weighted average of the nonzero
   146	  real quotients. This proves the Rayleigh identity with $-E_s$ on the left. The
   147	  following negative upper bound justifies writing that value as
   148	  $\lambda_{\Psi,s}^2$ in~\eqref{E:variational-real-rayleigh}.
   149	
   150	  Proposition~\ref{P:compact-original-common-trial} supplies, for this original
   151	  $\Psi$, one unit compactly supported $w$ and a finite plateau mask with a
   152	  common strictly negative upper bound $\epsilon_0 > 0$. Its trial has support
   153	  in $B_{2L}$; choose its plateau radius $R_0 \ge 2L$. The unmasked form on this
   154	  same $w$ is no larger. Consequently, $-M \le E_s \le -\epsilon_0 < 0$, and
   155	  $\sqrt{\epsilon_0} \le \lambda_{\Psi,s} \le \sqrt M$. Comparing identical unit
   156	  form tests gives $|E_s-E_t| \le \|h_s-h_t\|_\infty$ and therefore
   157	  \[
   158	    |\lambda_{\Psi,s}-\lambda_{\Psi,t}|
   159	    \le \frac{C_\Psi}{2\sqrt{\epsilon_0}}|s-t|.
   160	  \]
   161	  This also proves positivity and finiteness of $I_\Psi$. No compact-potential
   162	  spectral theorem was applied to $H_s$. This proves
   163	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-unmasked-rate}.
   164	\end{proof}

     2	\label{S:spatial-occupation-foundation}
     3	
     4	Retain a nonzero original covariance from Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} with its
     5	amplitude. Set $a = \alpha_0$, $k = 3-\alpha > 1$, $q = 4-\alpha = k+1$ and $D =
     6	q-2a > 0$. The scalar $D$ is fixed. All profiles are real. The original positive
     7	temporal exponent and threshold imply $\alpha < 2$; this is the strict

    11	
    12	\begin{lemma}[The physical two-point integral]\label{L:spatial-physical-pair}
    13	  The positive measure $\nu(\ud x,\ud y) = \ud x\,\Gamma(\ud y)$ is
    14	  sigma-finite. For nonnegative functions define
    15	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-physical-pair}
    16	    B_\Gamma(f,h)=\int f(x)h(x-y)\nu(\ud x,\ud y)
    17	  \end{equation}
    18	  initially as an extended nonnegative integral, using finite Borel
    19	  representatives of Lebesgue classes. Its value is representative independent.
    20	  Lebesgue-a.e. convergence transfers to $\nu$-a.e. convergence at both
    21	  positions $x$ and $x-y$.
    22	\end{lemma}
    23	
    24	\begin{proof}
    25	  Local finiteness of $\Gamma$ gives sigma-finiteness on exhausting balls, and
    26	  Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite. If $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue null, Tonelli
    27	  applied first in $x$ gives $\nu\{x\in N\} = 0$ and $\nu\{x-y\in N\} = 0$,
    28	  because every fixed translate of $N$ is null. An arbitrary Lebesgue null set
    29	  has a Borel null superset. Thus, arbitrary versions are measurable in the
    30	  $\nu$ completion with the same value, and the same observation applies to the
    31	  exceptional sets of a.e. convergence. Signed pairings will be used only after
    32	  absolute convergence. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-physical-pair}.
    33	\end{proof}
    34	
    35	Put $A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g) = B_\Gamma(g^2,g^2)$ and $b(g) = \|\nabla g\|_2^2$ on
    36	$H^1$; initially $A_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is used only for smooth compact profiles
    37	before the extension below. For smooth compact $z$, write $U_z = \Gamma*z$ in
    38	its usual pointwise sense.
    39	
    40	\begin{lemma}[Smooth temporal controls]\label{L:spatial-static-controls}
    41	  For every nonnegative nonzero $z \in C_c^\infty(\R^d)$, let
    42	  \[
    43	    \lambda_z(c)^2=
    44	    \sup_{\substack{g\in H^1(\R^d;\R)\\\|g\|_2=1}}
    45	    \left(c\int U_zg^2-b(g)\right),\qquad c>0.
    46	  \]
    47	  This is positive and finite, and $\lambda_z$ is Lipschitz on every compact
    48	  positive $c$ interval. With the exact $M_a$
    49	  in~\eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass},
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-static-score}
    51	    S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}\ge
    52	    \lambda_z(1)-\frac{M_a}{2}B_\Gamma(z,z).
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	\end{lemma}
    55	
    56	\begin{proof}
    57	  Choose nonnegative nonzero $f \in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ and $s_0 = 1/2$. Let
    58	  $k_f(s_0) = \int_0^1|s_0-t|^{-a}f(t)\ud t > 0$. The smooth test $\Psi(t,x) =
    59	  cf(t)z(x)/k_f(s_0)$ has mean $cU_z$ at $s_0$.
    60	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-unmasked-rate} gives boundedness of this
    61	  potential, the displayed real Rayleigh formula, and a positive rate for every
    62	  $c > 0$. Comparing identical unit tests makes $\lambda_z(c)^2$ Lipschitz with
    63	  constant $\|U_z\|_\infty$. On a positive compact interval its rate has a
    64	  positive floor by monotonicity, giving the square-root Lipschitz bound.
    65	
    66	  Use the nonincreasing smooth cutoff $\chi$ constructed in the proof of
    67	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-remove-mask}. For integers $n \ge 4$, set on
    68	  $(0,1)$
    69	  \[
    70	    f_n(t)=f_a(t)\chi(1/(nt))\chi(1/(n(1-t))),\qquad
    71	    k_n(s)=\int_0^1|s-t|^{-a}f_n(t)\ud t.
    72	  \]
    73	  Extend $f_n$ by zero. It is smooth compact, vanishes near both endpoints, is
    74	  nonzero, and increases to $f_a$. Thus, $\Psi_n = f_n\otimes z$ is a positive
    75	  smooth control. Monotone convergence
    76	  and~\eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential} give $k_n(s)\uparrow1$ for every
    77	  $s \in [0,1]$. Since the kernel is at least one on the unit square off its
    78	  null diagonal, $0 < c_0: = \int_0^1f_4 \le k_n(s) \le 1$. The mean is
    79	  $k_n(s)U_z$; hence its rate is $\lambda_z(k_n(s))$, converging to
    80	  $\lambda_z(1)$ and bounded by that finite number. Dominated convergence gives
    81	  $I_{\Psi_n} \to \lambda_z(1)$.
    82	
    83	  The Gaussian cost is exactly the nonnegative Tonelli pairing
    84	  \[
    85	    v_{\Psi_n}=B_\Gamma(z,z)\int_0^1f_n(s)k_n(s)\ud s.
    86	  \]
    87	  Its time integrand increases to $f_a$, so the cost tends to
    88	  $M_aB_\Gamma(z,z)$. The spatial factor is finite and positive: its smooth
    89	  compact autocorrelation is positive near zero, and homogeneity scales any
    90	  origin-centered ball of positive $\Gamma$ mass to every other positive radius.
    91	  Such a ball exists by exhaustion. Take the limit of the individual
    92	  inequalities $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}} \ge I_{\Psi_n}-v_{\Psi_n}/2$. The variational
    93	  expression differences need not increase. No control depends on original large
    94	  time and no rough stochastic evolution has been used. This proves
    95	  Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-static-controls}.
    96	\end{proof}

    98	The next estimate also allows zero covariance and does not use the finiteness
    99	of $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$.
   100	
   101	\begin{lemma}[Deterministic Fourier bound for the spatial energy]
   102	  \label{L:spatial-fourier-bound}
   103	  Under Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, allowing $\Gamma=0$, let
   104	  $g\in C_c^\infty(\R^d;\R)$ satisfy $\|g\|_2=1$ and put
   105	  $b=\|\nabla g\|_2^2$. Then $b>0$ and
   106	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-fourier-bound}
   107	    0\le A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)
   108	    \le 2^{1+\alpha}R_\alpha b^{\alpha/2},
   109	  \end{equation}
   110	  where $R_\alpha$ is defined in~\eqref{E:intro-spectral-mass}.
   111	\end{lemma}
   112	
   113	\begin{proof}
   114	  If $b=0$, smoothness makes $\nabla g=0$ everywhere. Thus, $g$ is constant,
   115	  and compact support forces $g=0$, contrary to $\|g\|_2=1$. Put $Q=g^2$ and
   116	  use the unnormalized Fourier transform
   117	  \[
   118	    \mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)=\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}Q(x)\ud x.
   119	  \]
   120	  In the unitary convention of Section~\ref{S:masked-covariance}, this is
   121	  $c_d^{-1}\widehat Q$, with $c_d=(2\pi)^{-d/2}$.
   122	  The autocorrelation
   123	  \[
   124	    c_Q(y)=\int_{\R^d}Q(x)Q(x-y)\ud x
   125	  \]
   126	  is smooth and compactly supported. Apply the distributional spectral
   127	  identity~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to this Schwartz function.
   128	  Its inner Fourier integral is $|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2$, since $Q$ is real.
   129	  Hence
   130	  \[
   131	    A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)=\int c_Q(y)\Gamma(\ud y)
   132	    =\int|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2\mu(\ud\xi).
   133	  \]
   134	  Both integrals are finite: $c_Q$ is compactly supported and $\Gamma$ is
   135	  Radon, while $|\mathcal{F}_0Q|^2$ is Schwartz and $\mu$ is tempered.
   136	  No density of either measure is required.
   137	
   138	  Since $\|Q\|_1=1$, we have $|\mathcal{F}_0Q|\le1$. Integration by parts
   139	  and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality give
   140	  \[
   141	    |\xi|\,|\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|
   142	    \le\|\nabla Q\|_1
   143	    \le2\|g\|_2\|\nabla g\|_2=2\sqrt b.
   144	  \]
   145	  Splitting into $|\xi|^2\le4b$ and $|\xi|^2>4b$ therefore yields
   146	  \[
   147	    |\mathcal{F}_0Q(\xi)|^2\le\frac{8b}{4b+|\xi|^2}.
   148	  \]
   149	  The deterministic resolvent calculation in the proof of
   150	  Lemma~\ref{L:damped-homogeneous-norms}, together
   151	  with~\eqref{E:intro-spectral-mass}, gives, for $q>0$,
   152	  \[
   153	    \mathcal{R}_\Gamma(q):=\int\frac{\mu(\ud\xi)}{q^2+|\xi|^2}
   154	    =q^{\alpha-2}R_\alpha<\infty.
   155	  \]
   156	  Consequently,
   157	  \[
   158	    A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)\le8b\mathcal{R}_\Gamma(2\sqrt b)
   159	    =2^{1+\alpha}R_\alpha b^{\alpha/2}.
   160	  \]
   161	  Nonnegativity follows from the spectral identity. If $\Gamma=0$, then
   162	  $\mu=0$ and both sides of~\eqref{E:spatial-fourier-bound} vanish. This proves
   163	  Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-fourier-bound}.
   164	\end{proof}
   165	
   166	\begin{proposition}[The finite smooth spatial ratio]
   167	  \label{P:spatial-smooth-ratio}
   168	  For real unit $g \in C_c^\infty(\R^d)$ put $R(g) =
   169	  A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)/b(g)^{\alpha/2}$. Its supremum $R_0$ over these profiles is
   170	  a positive finite real number, and
   171	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-smooth-score}
   172	    S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}\ge
   173	    k\left[
   174	    \frac{R(g)\alpha^{\alpha/2}}{8M_aq^{q/2}}
   175	    \right]^{1/k}.
   176	  \end{equation}
   177	\end{proposition}
   178	
   179	\begin{proof}
   180	  The gradient energy $b(g)$ is positive: a nonzero $L^2$ function with zero
   181	  weak gradient would have Fourier transform supported only at zero, and hence
   182	  would vanish. Its square is nonnegative nonzero smooth compact, so the
   183	  autocorrelation argument in the proof of
   184	  Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-static-controls} gives
   185	  $0 < A:=A_{\mathrm{sp}}(g)<\infty$. Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-fourier-bound} gives
   186	  $R(g)\le2^{1+\alpha}R_\alpha$ for every such profile. A normalized compact
   187	  bump supplies a positive ratio. Thus, $0<R_0<\infty$, independently of the
   188	  finiteness of $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$. It remains to prove the score inequality.
   189	  With $U_\ell g(x)=\ell^{d/2}g(\ell x)$, the physical changes of variables give
   190	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-dilation}
   191	    A_{\mathrm{sp}}(U_\ell g)=\ell^\alpha A,\qquad
   192	    b(U_\ell g)=\ell^2b(g).
   193	  \end{equation}
   194	  The factors in the first identity are $\ell^{2d}$ from the two squares,
   195	  $\ell^{-d}$ from $\ud x$, and $\ell^{\alpha-d}$ from the Radon pushforward.
   196	
   197	  For $\theta,\ell > 0$ choose the smooth control $z = \theta(U_\ell g)^2$. The
   198	  Rayleigh test $U_\ell g$ gives $\lambda_z(1)^2 \ge \theta\ell^\alpha
   199	  A-\ell^2b$, while $B_\Gamma(z,z) = \theta^2\ell^\alpha A$. For any $L > 0$,
   200	  put $u = \alpha/q > 0$ and choose
   201	  \[
   202	    \ell^2=uL^2/b,\qquad
   203	    \theta=(1+u)L^2/(\ell^\alpha A).
   204	  \]
   205	  The radicand is $L^2$. Lemma~\ref{L:spatial-static-controls} consequently
   206	  gives
   207	  \[
   208	    S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}\ge L-CL^q,\qquad
   209	    C=\frac{M_a(1+u)^2}{2R(g)u^{\alpha/2}}>0.
   210	  \]
   211	  Its maximum occurs at $L^k = 1/(qC)$ and is $(k/q)(qC)^{-1/k}$. Since $1+u =
   212	  4/q$, $1/(q^qC) = R(g)\alpha^{\alpha/2}/(8M_aq^{q/2})$,
   213	  proving~\eqref{E:spatial-smooth-score}. This argument retains the finite
   214	  real value $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$ fixed at the start of the section; only the
   215	  proof of $R_0<\infty$ is independent of that input. This proves
   216	  Proposition~\ref{P:spatial-smooth-ratio}.
   217	\end{proof}

1	\section{Covariance bounds for physically masked wave fields}
     2	\label{S:masked-covariance}
     3	
     4	We establish the covariance estimates needed for the operator construction.
     5	Throughout this section, Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} holds, $a = \alpha_0$, and
     6	$\Gamma \ne 0$. For zero spatial covariance, the spatial spectral measures and
     7	noise variances vanish; the purely temporal estimates remain valid independently
     8	of $\Gamma$. We use the unitary Fourier transform
     9	\[
    10	  \widehat{f}(\xi) = c_d\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\ud x,
    11	  \qquad c_d = (2\pi)^{-d/2}.
    12	\]
    13	The spectral convention in Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} means that, for every
    14	complex Schwartz test $\varphi$,
    15	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-spectral-convention}
    16	  \int_{\R^d}\varphi(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
    17	  = \int_{\R^d}\left(\int_{\R^d}e^{i\xi\cdot x}
    18	  \varphi(x)\ud x\right)\mu(\ud\xi).
    19	\end{equation}
    20	This is an identity of distribution pairings. We will not interchange two
    21	infinite measures in the associated oscillatory expression.
    22	
    23	A positive tempered Radon measure has polynomial mass growth. Indeed, choose a
    24	nonnegative compact smooth test that is at least one on the unit ball, and apply
    25	a defining Schwartz seminorm bound for the distribution to its dilations. Its
    26	mass on a ball of radius $R \ge 1$ is bounded by a power of $R$. Summation over
    27	dyadic shells then gives integrability of $(1+|x|)^{-N}$ for some $N$, and hence
    28	absolute integrability of every Schwartz test. These facts apply to both
    29	$\Gamma$ and $\mu$. Smooth cutoffs converge in the Schwartz topology, so these
    30	integrals agree with the tempered pairings.
    31	
    32	\subsection{Translated spectral growth and physical masks}
    33	
    34	\begin{proposition}[Translated spectral mass]\label{P:masked-spectral-growth}
    35	  Put
    36	  \[
    37	    M_\Gamma = \int_{\R^d}e^{-|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x),
    38	    \qquad C_\Gamma = \frac{eM_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d}.
    39	  \]
    40	  Then $0 < M_\Gamma < \infty$, and for $y \in \R^d$ and $r > 0$,
    41	  \begin{align}
    42	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    43	    &= \left(\frac{r}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^d
    44	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}\Gamma(\ud x),
    45	    \label{E:masked-gaussian-transform}\\
    46	    0 \le \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    47	    &\le \frac{r^\alpha M_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d},
    48	    \qquad \mu(B(y,r)) \le C_\Gamma r^\alpha.
    49	    \label{E:masked-translated-ball}
    50	  \end{align}
    51	  The ball may be open or closed.
    52	\end{proposition}
    53	
    54	\begin{proof}
    55	  Temperedness gives finiteness of $M_\Gamma$. Its positivity follows from
    56	  $\Gamma \ne 0$. To check the Fourier constant, set $J(b) = \int_\R
    57	  e^{-Ax^2}e^{ibx}\ud x$ for $A > 0$. Squaring the real Gaussian integral and
    58	  using polar coordinates gives $J(0) = \sqrt{\pi/A}$. Differentiation and
    59	  integration by parts give $J'(b) = -bJ(b)/(2A)$. Therefore, $J(b) =
    60	  \sqrt{\pi/A}e^{-b^2/(4A)}$. Taking products over the coordinates gives
    61	  \[
    62	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{i(\xi-y)\cdot x}\ud x
    63	    = \left(\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}}r\right)^d e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}.
    64	  \]
    65	  Apply~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to the single Schwartz test
    66	  $e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}$ to obtain \eqref{E:masked-gaussian-transform}.
    67	  Its left side is nonnegative. Taking the absolute value on the right removes
    68	  the complex phase because $\Gamma$ is nonnegative. The pushforward of $\Gamma$
    69	  by $x \mapsto rx$ assigns mass $r^{\alpha-d}\Gamma(A)$ to a Borel set $A$.
    70	  Thus,
    71	  \[
    72	    \int e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x) = r^{\alpha-d}M_\Gamma.
    73	  \]
    74	  This proves the Gaussian bound. On either ball $B(y,r)$ the integrand
    75	  $e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}$ is at least $e^{-1}$, proving the mass bound. This proves
    76	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-spectral-growth}.
    77	\end{proof}
    78	
    79	Choose and fix a real nonzero Schwartz function $\zeta$. For $R > 0$ put
    80	$\zeta_R(x) = \zeta(x/R)$, $k_R = \widehat{\zeta_R}$ and $L =
    81	\|\widehat{\zeta}\|_1$. Then $k_R(u) = R^d\widehat{\zeta}(Ru)$ and $\|k_R\|_1 =
    82	L > 0$. Define
    83	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-auxiliary-measure}
    84	  \nu_R(\ud\eta) = \rho_R(\eta)\ud\eta,
    85	  \qquad \rho_R(\eta) = c_d^2L\int |k_R(\xi-\eta)|\mu(\ud\xi).
    86	\end{equation}
    87	
    88	\begin{proposition}[Auxiliary mask norm]\label{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}
    89	  The measure $\nu_R$ is even, tempered and Radon, with
    90	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-auxiliary-growth}
    91	    \nu_R(B(y,r)) \le c_d^2L^2C_\Gamma r^\alpha
    92	  \end{equation}
    93	  for all $y \in \R^d$ and $r > 0$, uniformly in $R > 0$. If $H$ is a separable
    94	  complex Hilbert space and $F$ is an $H$-valued Schwartz function, then
    95	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-hilbert-fourier}
    96	    \int \|\widehat{\zeta_RF}(\xi)\|_H^2\mu(\ud\xi)
    97	    \le \int \|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_H^2\nu_R(\ud\eta).
    98	  \end{equation}
    99	  For a real $H$, the same assertion holds after complexification.
   100	\end{proposition}
   101	
   102	\begin{proof}
   103	  Schwartz decay of $k_R$ and polynomial growth of $\mu$ show that

   139	\subsection{Temporal completion and the original noise}
   140	
   141	\begin{lemma}[Temporal covariance completion]\label{L:masked-time-completion}
   142	  Let $T > 0$. The form
   143	  \[
   144	    \langle f,g\rangle_a
   145	    = \int_0^T\int_0^T f(t)g(s)|t-s|^{-a}\ud t\ud s
   146	  \]
   147	  is positive semidefinite on real compact smooth tests. Its null-quotient
   148	  completion $H_a$ is separable. The inclusion of tests extends continuously
   149	  from $L^2(0,T)$, with
   150	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-time-schur}
   151	    \|f\|_a^2 \le \frac{2T^{1-a}}{1-a}\|f\|_2^2.
   152	  \end{equation}
   153	  In its complexification the norm is given by the same double integral with
   154	  $f(t)\overline{f(s)}$. In particular, bounded measurable amplitudes on a
   155	  subinterval, extended by zero, belong to this completion.
   156	\end{lemma}
   157	
   158	\begin{proof}
   159	  Write $\Gamma_E$ for Euler's Gamma function. Away from the null diagonal,
   160	  \[
   161	    |t-s|^{-a} = \frac1{\Gamma_E(a)}\int_0^\infty
   162	    \lambda^{a-1}e^{-\lambda|t-s|}\ud\lambda.
   163	  \]
   164	  This follows by substitution in the defining Gamma integral. Moreover,
   165	  \[
   166	    e^{-\lambda|t-s|}
   167	    = \int_{-\infty}^{\min(t,s)}2\lambda
   168	    e^{-\lambda(t-u)}e^{-\lambda(s-u)}\ud u.
   169	  \]
   170	  For each $\lambda > 0$ its quadratic form is an integral of a square. All
   171	  exchanges for compact smooth tests are absolutely integrable because the
   172	  kernel row integral is at most $2T^{1-a}/(1-a)$. The same bound and $2|xy| \le
   173	  |x|^2+|y|^2$ prove~\eqref{E:masked-time-schur}. A countable $L^2$-dense family
   174	  of compact smooth tests is consequently dense in $H_a$, proving separability.
   175	  The complex quadratic form is the sum of those of the real and imaginary
   176	  parts, since symmetry cancels the imaginary cross term. Thus, the same bound
   177	  holds after complexification. Smooth density in $L^2$, together with the Schur
   178	  bound on the absolute bilinear form, extends the inclusion and the integral
   179	  identity to $L^2$. This includes the stated interval amplitudes. This proves
   180	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   181	\end{proof}

   183	Let $\mathcal{D}$ consist of finite sums $F(t,x) = \sum_j\tau_j(t)f_j(x)$ with
   184	real $\tau_j \in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ and real Schwartz $f_j$. These give
   185	$H_a$-valued Schwartz functions of $x$. Let $W$ denote the original real
   186	isonormal noise in~\eqref{E:cov}.

   250	define multiplication by $\zeta_R$ on the original noise quotient. Nor does the
   251	finite linear Gaussian comparison assert a covariance comparison for nonlinear
   252	wave solutions. The auxiliary and original test norms need not dominate one

   257	\begin{proposition}[A physical mask need not preserve noise-null tests]
   258	  \label{P:masked-quotient-obstruction}
   259	  In the admissible case $d = 2$, $\alpha = 1$, $0 < a < 1$ and $\Gamma =
   260	  \delta_0(\ud x_1)\ud x_2$, there is a real compact smooth mask $\zeta$ such
   261	  that no finite $C$ satisfies $\E W(\zeta F)^2 \le C\E W(F)^2$ for every
   262	  compact smooth test $F$.
   263	\end{proposition}
   264	
   265	\begin{proof}
   266	  Fourier inversion on Schwartz tests gives $\mu =
   267	  (2\pi)^{-1}\ud\xi_1\delta_0(\ud\xi_2)$ in the stated spectral convention. The
   268	  measure $\Gamma$ is nonnegative, even, positive definite and tempered, with
   269	  $\Gamma(cA) = c\Gamma(A)$. It therefore satisfies Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}
   270	  with $\alpha = 1$. This is not spatial white noise in dimension two. For real
   271	  compact smooth $g$, its spatial covariance is, by ordinary Fubini,
   272	  \[
   273	    V(g) = \int_\R\left(\int_\R g(x_1,x_2)\ud x_2\right)^2\ud x_1.
   274	  \]
   275	  Choose real even $\chi \in C_c^\infty(\R)$ equal to one on $[-1,1]$ and zero
   276	  outside $[-2,2]$. For example, on $1 < r = |x| < 2$ use
   277	  \[
   278	    \chi(x) = \frac{e^{-1/(2-r)}}{e^{-1/(2-r)}+e^{-1/(r-1)}}.
   279	  \]
   280	  The endpoint exponentials vanish to every order, so the plateau pastes
   281	  smoothly. Let $I_\chi = \int(\chi')^2 > 0$ and $J_\chi = \int\chi^4 > 0$.
   282	  Positivity of $I_\chi$ follows because $\chi$ is not constant, and $J_\chi \ge
   283	  2$. Put $g(x) = \chi(x_1)\chi''(x_2)$ and $\zeta(x) = \chi(x_1)\chi(x_2)$.
   284	  Their unmasked marginal vanishes since $\int\chi'' = 0$, whereas integration
   285	  by parts gives the masked marginal $-I_\chi\chi(x_1)^2$. Thus, $V(g) = 0$ and
   286	  $V(\zeta g) = J_\chi I_\chi^2 > 0$. For a nonzero nonnegative $\tau \in
   287	  C_c^\infty(0,T)$, set $F(t,x) = \tau(t)g(x)$. The temporal factor
   288	  $\|\tau\|_a^2$ is finite and strictly positive because its nonnegative
   289	  integrand is positive on a set of positive two-dimensional measure.

   291	  positive. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:masked-quotient-obstruction}.
   292	\end{proof}

   294	\subsection{Temporal modulation and continuous wave factors}
   295	
   296	Write $\langle x\rangle = \sqrt{1+x^2}$. Let $I = [s,s+h] \subset [0,T]$, with
   297	$0 < h \le 1$. Norms below are those of the complexified temporal completion in
   298	Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   299	
   300	\begin{lemma}[Modulated amplitudes]\label{L:masked-temporal-modulation}
   301	  Let $A \in C^1(I;\mathbb{C})$, $M = \sup_I|A|$ and $D = \sup_I|A'|$. For every
   302	  real $\omega$,
   303	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-temporal-modulation}
   304	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   305	    \le C_0(a)h^{2-a}(M+hD)^2\langle h\omega\rangle^{a-1},
   306	    \qquad C_0(a) = \frac{16}{1-a}.
   307	  \end{equation}
   308	  The bound is uniform in $T,s,h,A$ and $\omega$.
   309	\end{lemma}
   310	
   311	\begin{proof}
   312	  Put $c(v) = \int_s^{s+h-v}A(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u$ for $0 \le v \le h$.
   313	  Differentiation at the moving endpoint gives
   314	  \[
   315	    c'(v) = -A(s+h)\overline{A(s+h-v)}
   316	    +\int_s^{s+h-v}A'(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u.
   317	  \]
   318	  Thus, $c(h) = 0$, $|c(v)| \le hM^2$ and $|c'(v)| \le M^2+hMD$. Splitting the
   319	  covariance square into its two conjugate triangles gives
   320	  \[
   321	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   322	    = 2\operatorname{Re}\int_0^h v^{-a}e^{i\omega v}c(v)\ud v
   323	    = 2h^{2-a}\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1 y^{-a}e^{i\omega hy}f(y)\ud y,
   324	  \]
   325	  where $f(y) = c(hy)/h$. Set $K = M+hD$. Then $f(1) = 0$ and $|f|,|f'| \le
   326	  K^2$. If $K = 0$ the assertion is immediate. If $|\omega h| \le 1$, the last
   327	  integral is at most $K^2/(1-a)$ in absolute value, and $\langle\omega
   328	  h\rangle^{a-1} \ge 2^{(a-1)/2}$. The claimed constant is sufficient in this
   329	  case.
   330	
   331	  Now suppose $k = |\omega h| > 1$. On $[0,1/k]$ the integral is at most
   332	  $K^2k^{a-1}/(1-a)$. On $[1/k,1]$, integrate the exponential by parts. The
   333	  endpoint at one vanishes, while the other endpoint contributes at most
   334	  $K^2k^{a-1}$. The derivative integral, divided by $k$, is bounded by
   335	  \[
   336	    \frac{K^2}k\left(a\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a-1}\ud y
   337	    +\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a}\ud y\right)
   338	    \le K^2 k^{a-1}\left(1+\frac1{1-a}\right).
   339	  \]
   340	  Here $k^{-1} \le k^{a-1}$ since $a > 0$. The total is at most
   341	  $4K^2k^{a-1}/(1-a)$. Finally, $k^{a-1} \le \sqrt{2}\langle\omega
   342	  h\rangle^{a-1}$ and $8\sqrt{2} \le 16$. Including the factor $2h^{2-a}$ proves
   343	  the bound for either sign of $\omega$. This proves
   344	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-temporal-modulation}.
   345	\end{proof}
   346	
   347	\begin{lemma}[Correlated trigonometric products]\label{L:masked-trig-products}
   348	  Let $r,\rho \ge 0$. Let $P_r$ be either $\cos(rt)$ or $\sin(rt)$, and let
   349	  $Q_\rho$ be either $\cos(\rho t)$ or $\sin(\rho t)$. With the amplitude and
   350	  constant above,
   351	  \begin{align}
   352	    \|1_IAP_rQ_\rho\|_a^2
   353	    &\le C_0(a)h^{2-a}(M+hD)^2\mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho),
   354	    \label{E:masked-trig-products}\\
   355	    \mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho)
   356	    &:= \langle h(r-\rho)\rangle^{a-1}
   357	    +\langle h(r+\rho)\rangle^{a-1}.
   358	    \label{E:masked-frequency-pair}
   359	  \end{align}
   360	\end{lemma}
   361	
   362	\begin{proof}
   363	  Expanding the two trigonometric factors gives four complex exponential modes
   364	  with frequencies $\sigma r+\tau\rho$, $\sigma,\tau \in \{-1,1\}$, and
   365	  coefficients of absolute value $1/4$. In a Hilbert space,
   366	  \[
   367	    \left\|\sum_j c_jv_j\right\|^2
   368	    \le \left(\sum_j|c_j|\right)\sum_j|c_j|\|v_j\|^2.
   369	  \]
   370	  The first coefficient sum is one. Apply
   371	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-temporal-modulation} to each mode. Two frequencies have
   372	  absolute value $|r-\rho|$ and two have absolute value $r+\rho$. This gives one
   373	  half of the asserted right side, and hence the bound. Repeated or zero
   374	  frequencies are permitted; no orthogonality or independence of the modes is
   375	  used. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:masked-trig-products}.
   376	\end{proof}

   270	\begin{proposition}[Intrinsic variational lower bounds]
   271	  \label{P:variational-positive-scores}
   272	  For $c > 0$, the set of variational values
   273	  $\{cI_\Psi-v_\Psi/2:\Psi\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}\}$ is nonempty and
   274	  bounded above. Its finite real supremum $S_c^{\mathrm{pos}}$ is positive and
   275	  satisfies
   276	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-score-homogeneity}
   277	    S_c^{\mathrm{pos}}=c^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}S_1^{\mathrm{pos}},
   278	    \qquad
   279	    Q_2\ge S_2^{\mathrm{pos}},
   280	  \end{equation}
   281	  where $Q_2$ is the original point liminf. The coefficient-one value is an
   282	  auxiliary variational value; no first-moment or source-constant identification
   283	  is asserted.
   284	\end{proposition}
   285	
   286	\begin{proof}
   287	  Write $k = 3-\alpha > 0$, $q = 4-\alpha = k+1$ and $m = q/k > 1$. Fix one
   288	  $\Psi_0$ from the nonempty class and put $I_0 = I_{\Psi_0} > 0$, $v_0 =
   289	  v_{\Psi_0} > 0$. Positivity of the latter is
   290	  Lemma~\ref{L:compact-raw-profile}. For $r_0 = (I_0/v_0)^{1/k} > 0$, which need
   291	  not be less than one, the exact real-power identity gives
   292	  \[
   293	    I_{D_{r_0}\Psi_0}-v_{D_{r_0}\Psi_0}/2
   294	    =r_0I_0-r_0^qv_0/2=r_0I_0/2>0.
   295	  \]
   296	  This positive value is obtained from a smooth nonnegative control.
   297	
   298	  For $c > 0$ put $r_c = c^{1/k}$ and $K_c = c^m > 0$.
   299	  Lemma~\ref{L:variational-control-dilation} and the exact scalar powers give,
   300	  for every $\Psi$,
   301	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-score-set-scaling}
   302	    cI_{D_{r_c}\Psi}-v_{D_{r_c}\Psi}/2
   303	    =K_c(I_\Psi-v_\Psi/2).
   304	  \end{equation}
   305	  Since $D_{r_c}$ is a bijection of the entire class, the whole set of
   306	  variational values with coefficient $c$ is $K_c$ times the whole
   307	  coefficient-one set of variational values.
   308	
   309	  We prove boundedness before taking finite-real suprema. The independent
   310	  Theorem~\ref{T:full-upper}, for the \emph{same canonical solution}, gives
   311	  \[
   312	    \E|u(T,0)|^2\le e(T+2)^d e^{C_{\mathrm{up}}T^\kappa},
   313	    \qquad T\ge1,\quad C_{\mathrm{up}}<\infty.
   314	  \]
   315	  Its prefactor is negligible: choose $\epsilon = \kappa/2 > 0$, use $\log T \le
   316	  (T^\epsilon-1)/\epsilon$ and $\log(T+2) \le \log T+\log3$ for $T \ge 1$, and
   317	  divide by $T^\kappa$. Thus, the original point limsup is at most
   318	  $C_{\mathrm{up}}$. One fixed test/mask lower bound gives a finite lower bound
   319	  for $Q_2$, so $Q_2$ is finite. By~\eqref{E:variational-unmasked-point-lower}
   320	  every coefficient-two variational expression is at most this same $Q_2 \le
   321	  C_{\mathrm{up}}$, uniformly in $\Psi$.
   322	  Equation~\eqref{E:variational-score-set-scaling} at $c = 2$ consequently
   323	  bounds all coefficient-one variational values by $C_{\mathrm{up}}/K_2$. The
   324	  nonempty set has a finite real supremum $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}} > 0$ by the
   325	  positive test above.
   326	
   327	  For general $c$, set equality and $K_c > 0$ show that $K_cS_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$
   328	  is the supremum: it is an upper bound, and every smaller number is exceeded by
   329	  $K_c$ times a coefficient-one variational expression within the corresponding
   330	  positive distance of its supremum. This proves finiteness, positivity and the
   331	  first identity in~\eqref{E:variational-score-homogeneity}. Taking the
   332	  numerical supremum of the coefficient-two lower bounds proves the second.

   334	  is only a comparison of auxiliary variational values. It is not a Jensen
   335	  improvement without a first-moment identification. This proves
   336	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-positive-scores}.
   337	\end{proof}
   338	
   339	For $\Gamma = 0$, the mean, original variance and Rayleigh rate are zero. Set
   340	all these variational values to zero; the free canonical solution $u = 1$ has
   341	the corresponding zero moment rate. Strict positivity above is restricted to

   121	These counts describe the package. They are not a percentage of the paper.
   122	The 28 whole results and 18 narrower results are deterministic lemmas,
   123	propositions and corollaries used inside the analytic argument, and the
   124	occupation ceiling `T:intrinsic-occupation-ceiling` (a narrower result: both
   125	forms with the exact constant, for `S_c^pos`; `C_2 <= U_2` not formalized);
   126	the other three main theorems are not formalized.
   127	
   128	## Reading a statement
   129	
   130	For each declaration, check three things against the paper:
   131	
   132	1. the hypotheses match what the paper has available at that point;
   133	2. the conclusion is what the paper uses next;
   134	3. parameter ranges, strict versus non-strict inequalities and quantifier
   135	   order agree.
   136	
   137	The [statement ledger](docs/statement-ledger.md) records this for every row.
   138	`Audit/<module>/` prints the full elaborated types, so the statements can be
   139	read without opening an editor.
   140	
   141	## Not yet included
   142	
   143	Three development modules use a Gaussian-chaos library that is not yet
   144	public: normalized Gaussian coordinates, vector Gaussian projection and
   145	colored vector words. They are checked in the private development record
   146	and will be added here when that library is released.
   147	
   148	## Possible next steps
   149	
   150	- the finite pair-partition counts behind the two-chain integrals;
   151	- a reusable Laplace-to-time growth lemma, with its analytic inputs as
   152	  hypotheses;
   153	- the constant and exponent algebra of the main upper and lower bounds.
